full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique J. This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 16.02.2002 passed by the High Court Division Writ Petition No. 1934 of 1995 discharging the Rule. 

 5. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties discharged the Rule. Thus, the writ petitioners preferred appeal upon getting leave. 

 6. Mr. Md. Zafarullah Chowdhury, learned Counsel appearing for the appellants submits that the High Court Division erred in law in deciding the question of title holding that the appellants heave no title in the disputed property. He submits that the High Court Division committed error of law in holding that he property, in question, stood acquired by the Government under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act inasmuch as there was no material on record to support the finding that the interest of Gyonotosh Ray Chowdhury in the said property stood acquired under the said Act. He further submits that the Government has requisitioned the property, in question, upon issuing notice to the predecessor-in-interest of the appellants. Therefore, the High Court Division was wrong in not holding that the Government is stopped from claiming the property as khas land. He further submits that the High Court Division misread the gazette notification issued under section 3 of the Stated Acquisition and Tenancy Act and came to a wrong finding that the interest of Gaynotosh Roy Chowdhury was acquired in 1954. 

 7. Mr. Biswjith Debnath learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing for the respondents, submits that the disputed jalamahal was acquired by the Government under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1954 and the right, title, interest and possession of the same was vested in the Government free from all encumbrances, the High Court Division, upon proper appreciation of the materials on record, discharged the Rule. 

 (ii)	all interest of all rent-receivers whose properties are, for the time being, under the management of the Court of Wards under the Court of Wards Act, 1879, in their respective estates, taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies, as the case may be, including all their interests in all sub-soil and rights to minerals in such estates, taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies. 

 11. Therefore, on combined reading of section 21(16) and section 3 of the Act, it is evident that with the publication of Gazette notification under section 3 of the Act all interests of the rent receivers, in the respective estates, taluks, tenders, holdings or tenancies, as the case may be, in any district, part of a district or local areas and all interests of all rent-receivers whose properties are, for the time being under management of the Court of Wards under the Court of Wards Act, 1879, in their respective estates, taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies, as the case may be, including all their interests in all sub-soil and rights to minerals in such estates, talkus, tenures, holdings or tenancies vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and that under section 2(16) any land which is under water at any time of the year falls within the definition of land. 

 16. Considering, the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that the High Court Division did not commit any error of law in discharging the Rule.
